[Textbook misprint: the question names the "Bracket series". The series is the BRACKETT series, named after Frederick Brackett, and the book itself spells it correctly in Section 15.5 and in Fig. 15.4. The answer is unaffected.]

The series limit of a series is its shortest wavelength, reached when \(m \rightarrow \infty\). Putting \(1/m^{2} = 0\) in Rydberg's formula for hydrogen,

\(\dfrac{1}{\lambda} = R_H\left(\dfrac{1}{n^{2}} - \dfrac{1}{m^{2}}\right) \rightarrow \dfrac{1}{\lambda_{\text{limit}}} = \dfrac{R_H}{n^{2}}\), i.e. \(\lambda_{\text{limit}} = \dfrac{n^{2}}{R_H}\)

So the series limit is proportional to \(n^{2}\). The Lyman series has \(n = 1\), so its limit is \(1/R_H = 911.6\) Å, and every other limit is simply \(n^{2}\) times this value.

Balmer \((n = 2)\): \(\lambda = 2^{2} \times 911.6 = 4 \times 911.6 = 3646\) Å

Paschen \((n = 3)\): \(\lambda = 3^{2} \times 911.6 = 9 \times 911.6 = 8204\) Å

Brackett \((n = 4)\): \(\lambda = 4^{2} \times 911.6 = 16 \times 911.6 = 14586\) Å

**Series limits: 3646 Å, 8204 Å and 14586 Å** (about 14585 Å to the accuracy of the data).

An alpha particle is the nucleus \(^{4}_{2}\text{He}\), so it contains \(Z = 2\) protons and \(N = 2\) neutrons. Since the mass given, 4.00151 u, is that of the alpha particle itself (a bare nucleus), the binding energy follows from the NUCLEAR mass defect,

\(E_B = \left[Zm_p + Nm_n - m_{\alpha}\right]c^{2}\)

Using \(m_p = 1.00728\) u and \(m_n = 1.00866\) u from the data given with the exercises,

\(E_B = \left[2 \times 1.00728 + 2 \times 1.00866 - 4.00151\right] \times 931.5\)

\(= \left[2.01456 + 2.01732 - 4.00151\right] \times 931.5\)

\(= 0.03037 \times 931.5\)

\(= 28.29\ \text{MeV}\)

**The binding energy of an alpha particle is 28.29 MeV**, i.e. about 7.07 MeV per nucleon.

The number of revolutions is the frequency of revolution multiplied by the time, \(N = f \times t\), where \(f = \dfrac{\mathrm{v}_n}{2\pi r_n}\).

For hydrogen \((Z = 1)\) in the second orbit \((n = 2)\):

\(\mathrm{v}_2 = \dfrac{e^{2}}{2\varepsilon_0 h n} = \dfrac{(1.602 \times 10^{-19})^{2}}{2 \times 8.854 \times 10^{-12} \times 6.626 \times 10^{-34} \times 2} = 1.094 \times 10^{6}\ \text{m s}^{-1}\)

\(r_2 = \dfrac{n^{2}h^{2}\varepsilon_0}{\pi m_e e^{2}} = 4 \times 5.293 \times 10^{-11} = 2.117 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{m}\)

\(\therefore f = \dfrac{1.094 \times 10^{6}}{2\pi \times 2.117 \times 10^{-10}} = 8.221 \times 10^{14}\ \text{revolutions per second}\)

\(\therefore N = 8.221 \times 10^{14} \times 10^{-8}\)

**\(N = 8.221 \times 10^{6}\) revolutions**

For \(^{244}_{95}\text{Am}\), \(Z = 95\) and \(A = 244\), so the number of neutrons is \(N = A - Z = 244 - 95 = 149\).

The mass given, 244.06428 u, is the ATOMIC mass, so the binding energy is obtained with the hydrogen atom mass \(m_H\), which carries the 95 atomic electrons on the other side of the equation:

\(E_B = \left[Zm_H + Nm_n - {}^{A}_{Z}M\right]c^{2}\)

\(= \left[95 \times 1.007825 + 149 \times 1.00866 - 244.06428\right] \times 931.5\)

\(= \left[95.743375 + 150.29034 - 244.06428\right] \times 931.5\)

\(= 1.969435 \times 931.5 = 1834.53\ \text{MeV}\)

The binding energy per nucleon is

\(\dfrac{E_B}{A} = \dfrac{1834.53}{244} = 7.52\ \text{MeV}\)

**The binding energy per nucleon of \(^{244}_{95}\text{Am}\) is about 7.5 MeV.**

[Textbook answer-key error: the book prints 16.84 MeV. That value comes from combining a bare proton \((m_p = 1.00728\ \text{u})\) with ATOMIC masses for lithium and helium, which leaves one electron unaccounted for on the left-hand side: the two helium atoms carry 4 electrons while the lithium atom and a bare proton carry only 3. The printed answer is therefore too small by exactly one electron rest energy, 0.512 MeV. The correct energy released is 17.35 MeV, which is also the accepted laboratory Q value for the reaction \(^{7}\text{Li}(p,\alpha)\alpha\).]

The reaction is \(^{7}_{3}\text{Li} + p \rightarrow 2\alpha\), and the energy released is the difference in mass between the reactants and the products.

The electrons have to be counted consistently. The masses supplied are ATOMIC masses: the \(^{7}_{3}\text{Li}\) atom carries 3 electrons and each helium atom carries 2, so the two helium atoms on the right carry 4 electrons in all. The left-hand side therefore needs 4 electrons too, which means the proton must be entered as a hydrogen ATOM, \(m_H = 1.007825\) u.

\(Q = \left[m_{Li} + m_H - 2m_{He}\right]c^{2}\)

\(= \left[7.016 + 1.007825 - 2 \times 4.0026\right] \times 931.5\)

\(= \left[8.023825 - 8.0052\right] \times 931.5\)

\(= 0.018625 \times 931.5\)

\(= 17.35\ \text{MeV}\)

The same result follows from NUCLEAR masses: \((7.016 - 3m_e) + m_p - 2(4.0026 - 2m_e) = 0.01863\) u, again \(17.35\) MeV.

**The energy released is 17.35 MeV.**

[Textbook answer-key error: all three printed answers are wrong. The book gives a) 32.096 MeV, b) 172.485 MeV and c) 1.485 MeV; the masses supplied in the question give a) 31.82 MeV, b) 171.0 MeV and c) 0.96 MeV. Part (c) is the clearest case — it is a beta PLUS decay, so with atomic masses two electron masses must be subtracted rather than one, and the book's value is about half an MeV too large; 0.96 MeV agrees with the accepted \(Q(\beta^{+})\) of 0.9605 MeV for \(^{11}\text{C}\). For (a) and (b) the printed values could not be reproduced by any reading of the data; re-deriving from accepted atomic masses gives 31.83 MeV and 170.9 MeV, confirming the values above.]

In each case the energy released is \(Q = \left[\sum m_{\text{reactants}} - \sum m_{\text{products}}\right]c^{2}\), with \(1\ \text{u} = 931.5\ \text{MeV}\). All the masses supplied are ATOMIC masses.

**(a)** \(^{223}_{88}\text{Ra} \rightarrow {}^{209}_{82}\text{Pb} + {}^{14}_{6}\text{C}\)

The electrons balance \((88 = 82 + 6)\), so the atomic masses may be used directly.

\(Q = \left[223.0185 - 208.9811 - 14.00324\right] \times 931.5\)

\(= 0.03416 \times 931.5 = 31.82\ \text{MeV}\)

**(b)** \(^{236}_{92}\text{U} \rightarrow {}^{140}_{56}\text{Ba} + {}^{94}_{36}\text{Kr} + 2n\)

The electrons balance \((92 = 56 + 36)\); the two neutrons are added with \(m_n = 1.00866\) u.

\(Q = \left[236.0456 - 139.9106 - 93.9341 - 2 \times 1.00866\right] \times 931.5\)

\(= \left[2.2009 - 2.01732\right] \times 931.5 = 0.18358 \times 931.5 = 171.0\ \text{MeV}\)

**(c)** \(^{11}_{6}\text{C} \rightarrow {}^{11}_{5}\text{B} + e^{+} +\) neutrino

This is a beta plus decay. The carbon atom carries 6 electrons and the boron atom only 5, and a positron is created as well, so when atomic masses are used TWO electron masses must be subtracted:

\(Q = \left[m_C - m_B - 2m_e\right]c^{2} = \left[11.01143 - 11.0093 - 2 \times 0.00055\right] \times 931.5\)

\(= \left[0.00213 - 0.0011\right] \times 931.5 = 0.00103 \times 931.5 = 0.96\ \text{MeV}\)

**Energies released: (a) 31.82 MeV, (b) 171.0 MeV, (c) 0.96 MeV.**

The activity of a sample falls exponentially, \(A(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}\). The living sample fixes the activity the old sample had when it died, so

\(A_0 = 15.3\) and \(A(t) = 12.3\) decays per gram per minute

(the units cancel in the ratio, so they need not be converted).

\(e^{\lambda t} = \dfrac{A_0}{A(t)} = \dfrac{15.3}{12.3} = 1.2439\)

\(\therefore \lambda t = \ln(1.2439) = 0.21825\)

\(\therefore t = \dfrac{0.21825}{3.839 \times 10^{-12}} = 5.685 \times 10^{10}\ \text{s}\)

Converting to years, \(1\ \text{year} = 365 \times 24 \times 3600 = 3.154 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s}\):

\(t = \dfrac{5.685 \times 10^{10}}{3.154 \times 10^{7}} = 1803\ \text{years}\)

**The old sample is about 1803 years old.**

The disintegration rate is the activity \(A = \lambda N\).

**Decay constant.** \(T_{1/2} = 28\ \text{years} = 28 \times 3.154 \times 10^{7} = 8.830 \times 10^{8}\ \text{s}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{8.830 \times 10^{8}} = 7.848 \times 10^{-10}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

**Number of nuclei.** \(^{90}_{38}\text{Sr}\) has a gram atomic mass of 90 g, so 5 mg contains

\(N = \dfrac{5 \times 10^{-3}}{90} \times 6.022 \times 10^{23} = 3.346 \times 10^{19}\) nuclei

**Activity.**

\(A = \lambda N = 7.848 \times 10^{-10} \times 3.346 \times 10^{19}\)

**\(A = 2.626 \times 10^{10}\) disintegrations per second** \((\text{i.e. } 2.626 \times 10^{10}\ \text{Bq}\), about 0.71 Ci).

**Required activity.** \(1\ \text{Ci} = 3.7 \times 10^{10}\) decays per second, so

\(A = 10.0\ \text{mCi} = 10.0 \times 10^{-3} \times 3.7 \times 10^{10} = 3.7 \times 10^{8}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

**Decay constant.** \(T_{1/2} = 5.3\ \text{years} = 5.3 \times 3.154 \times 10^{7} = 1.671 \times 10^{8}\ \text{s}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{1.671 \times 10^{8}} = 4.146 \times 10^{-9}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

**Number of nuclei needed.** From \(A = \lambda N\),

\(N = \dfrac{A}{\lambda} = \dfrac{3.7 \times 10^{8}}{4.146 \times 10^{-9}} = 8.924 \times 10^{16}\) nuclei

**Mass.** The gram atomic mass of \(^{60}_{27}\text{Co}\) is 60 g, so

\(m = \dfrac{N}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} \times 60 = \dfrac{8.924 \times 10^{16}}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} \times 60\)

**\(m = 8.89 \times 10^{-6}\) g**, i.e. about 8.9 micrograms of \(^{60}_{27}\text{Co}\).

The activity decays as \(A(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}\), so between the two given instants, separated by \(30 - 20 = 10\) hours,

\(\dfrac{A(30)}{A(20)} = e^{-\lambda \times 10} = \dfrac{6.3 \times 10^{9}}{10^{10}} = 0.63\)

\(\therefore 10\lambda = -\ln(0.63) = 0.4620\)

\(\therefore \lambda = 0.04620\ \text{hour}^{-1}\)

**Half-life.**

\(T_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{\lambda} = \dfrac{0.693}{0.04620} = 15.0\ \text{hours}\)

**Initial number of atoms.** The activity at \(t = 0\) is obtained by running the decay back 20 hours from the first reading:

\(A_0 = A(20)\,e^{+20\lambda} = 10^{10} \times e^{0.9241} = 10^{10} \times 2.5195 = 2.5195 \times 10^{10}\) per hour

Since \(A_0 = \lambda N_0\), and both \(A_0\) and \(\lambda\) are expressed per hour,

\(N_0 = \dfrac{A_0}{\lambda} = \dfrac{2.5195 \times 10^{10}}{0.04620} = 5.45 \times 10^{11}\)

**Half-life \(= 15\) hours; initial number of radioactive atoms \(= 5.45 \times 10^{11}\).**

**(a) Decay constant and mean lifetime.**

\(T_{1/2} = 272\ \text{d} = 272 \times 24 \times 3600 = 2.350 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{0.693}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{2.350 \times 10^{7}} = 2.95 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

\(\tau = \dfrac{1}{\lambda} = 3.39 \times 10^{7}\ \text{s}\) (about 393 days)

**(b) Number of nuclei in the source.**

\(A = 2.0\ \mu\text{Ci} = 2.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 3.7 \times 10^{10} = 7.4 \times 10^{4}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

\(N = \dfrac{A}{\lambda} = \dfrac{7.4 \times 10^{4}}{2.95 \times 10^{-8}} = 2.51 \times 10^{12}\) nuclei

**(c) Activity after one year.**

\(t = 365\ \text{d}\), so \(\lambda t = 0.693 \times \dfrac{365}{272} = 0.9299\)

\(A(t) = A_0 e^{-\lambda t} = 2.0 \times e^{-0.9299} = 2.0 \times 0.3946\)

\(A(t) = 0.789\ \mu\text{Ci}\)

**Mean lifetime \(3.39 \times 10^{7}\) s, decay constant \(2.95 \times 10^{-8}\ \text{s}^{-1}\), \(2.51 \times 10^{12}\) nuclei, and the activity falls to \(0.789\ \mu\text{Ci}\) after one year.**

Let the activities of the two species be \(A_{32}(t)\) and \(A_{33}(t)\). At \(t = 0\), \(^{32}_{15}\text{P}\) accounts for 90% of the decays and \(^{33}_{15}\text{P}\) for the remaining 10%, so we may write \(A_{32}(0) = 0.9\) and \(A_{33}(0) = 0.1\) in any convenient unit.

The decay constants are

\(\lambda_{32} = \dfrac{0.693}{14.3} = 0.04846\ \text{d}^{-1}\), \(\lambda_{33} = \dfrac{0.693}{25.3} = 0.02739\ \text{d}^{-1}\)

The requirement is that the \(^{32}_{15}\text{P}\) share of the total falls to 15%:

\(\dfrac{0.9e^{-\lambda_{32}t}}{0.9e^{-\lambda_{32}t} + 0.1e^{-\lambda_{33}t}} = 0.15\)

Dividing numerator and denominator by \(e^{-\lambda_{33}t}\) and putting \(x = e^{-(\lambda_{32}-\lambda_{33})t}\),

\(\dfrac{0.9x}{0.9x + 0.1} = 0.15\)

\(0.9x = 0.135x + 0.015\), so \(0.765x = 0.015\) and \(x = 0.019608\)

\(\therefore (\lambda_{32} - \lambda_{33})\,t = -\ln(0.019608) = 3.9318\)

\(\lambda_{32} - \lambda_{33} = 0.04846 - 0.02739 = 0.02107\ \text{d}^{-1}\)

\(\therefore t = \dfrac{3.9318}{0.02107}\)

**\(t = 186.6\) days must elapse.**

**Decay constant of \(^{14}\text{C}\).** \(T_{1/2} = 5730\ \text{years} = 5730 \times 3.154 \times 10^{7} = 1.807 \times 10^{11}\ \text{s}\)

\(\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}} = \dfrac{0.693}{1.807 \times 10^{11}} = 3.836 \times 10^{-12}\ \text{s}^{-1}\)

**(a) Fraction of carbon atoms that were \(^{14}\text{C}\).** For one gram of carbon the activity is 0.255 Bq, so from \(A = \lambda N\),

\(N(^{14}\text{C}) = \dfrac{0.255}{3.836 \times 10^{-12}} = 6.65 \times 10^{10}\) atoms per gram

The total number of carbon atoms in one gram is \(\dfrac{6.022 \times 10^{23}}{12} = 5.018 \times 10^{22}\).

\(\text{fraction} = \dfrac{6.65 \times 10^{10}}{5.018 \times 10^{22}} = 1.32 \times 10^{-12}\)

That is, **about four \(^{14}\text{C}\) atoms in every \(3 \times 10^{12}\) carbon atoms.**

**(b) Age of the specimen.** The specimen gives 174 decays in one hour from 500 mg, so per gram

\(A = \dfrac{174}{3600 \times 0.5} = 0.0967\ \text{Bq g}^{-1}\)

When it died its activity per gram was the atmospheric value \(A_0 = 0.255\ \text{Bq g}^{-1}\). From \(A = A_0 e^{-\lambda t}\),

\(\lambda t = \ln\dfrac{0.255}{0.0967} = \ln(2.638) = 0.9700\)

\(t = \dfrac{0.9700}{3.836 \times 10^{-12}} = 2.529 \times 10^{11}\ \text{s}\)

\(t = \dfrac{2.529 \times 10^{11}}{3.154 \times 10^{7}}\)

**The specimen is about 8020 years old.**

**Energy needed in one day.** A thermal power of 3000 MW sustained for a day gives

\(E = Pt = 3000 \times 10^{6} \times (24 \times 3600) = 2.592 \times 10^{14}\ \text{J}\)

**Energy per fission.** \(1\ \text{MeV} = 10^{6} \times 1.602 \times 10^{-19} = 1.602 \times 10^{-13}\ \text{J}\), so

\(E_1 = 202.79 \times 1.602 \times 10^{-13} = 3.249 \times 10^{-11}\ \text{J}\)

**Number of fissions required.**

\(n = \dfrac{E}{E_1} = \dfrac{2.592 \times 10^{14}}{3.249 \times 10^{-11}} = 7.979 \times 10^{24}\)

**Mass of \(^{235}\text{U}\).** One mole of \(^{235}\text{U}\) is 235 g and contains \(6.022 \times 10^{23}\) nuclei, so

\(m = \dfrac{7.979 \times 10^{24}}{6.022 \times 10^{23}} \times 235 = 13.25 \times 235 = 3114\ \text{g}\)

**About 3.1 kg of \(^{235}\text{U}\) must undergo fission each day.**
